In one of the campaigns I'm GMing at the moment, a pathfinder campaign. The players are soon going to venture into the under dark, heading to save a priestess from a drow matron.

I find that random encounters are sometime stale and I hate to have combat for combats sake, because of this I tend to hand-wave a lot of overground travel. This doesn't seem right for the Under Dark.

The system I have created is simpleish.

I have made a set or cards, on them is written encounters, sights or terrain. There are also a load of cards with, Fork, passage down, dead end, etc.

There are three types of tunnel the characters might enter. Primary, Secondary, and Tertiary, these tunnels might open into caverns for encounters but in general they are as described below.

Primary Tunnels are about 15-20’ wide and have only a 5% chance of a random encounter. The encounter cards represent these tunnels. It takes 1D4 days to travel through each of these cards.

Secondary tunnels, take 1D6 days to travel along and have a 20% chance or a random encounter. they are narrower, 5-10’ wide and a difficult to travel along. Traveling along these tunnels, just allows you to reach the next primary tunnel essentially bypassing a dead end, or an obstacle the characters can’t overcome.

Tertiary tunnels are very narrow 2-5’ wide and have 50% chance of a random encounter. They take 1D10 days to travel along and are entered if the players still want to continue skipping a primary path card after already skipping one.

  • You place the cards in three piles, with the destination card at the bottom of a random pile.
  • Dead end means go back to last fork. Or move onto secondary path.
  • When you return to the primary path you must either go along it and deal with the next card or you can use a tertiary path.
  • Fork cards allow you to move into the other piles of cards.
  • You are always welcome to try and make you way back along your route to find another path at a fork, but you must reencounter all the obstacles (or what remains of them). So if you climbed down a lift shaft you must climb back up, and if you left the bodies of some slavers lying around, something might be there feasting on their remains.
  • You start with two weeks of rations, each travel roll allows with someone to make a survival check in order to gather more supplies, or the party can stop travelling for the day and everyone can make survival checks to gather more supplies.

They also might find a map which would allow you to look at the next few cards in each pile, or you might meet a traveling merchant who will tell you which pile the destination is in, if you can trust him

Let me know what you think. I think it should add a good survival element, and allow it to feel like the players are deciding where they go without having to plot out hundreds of miles of under dark tunnels.

Let me know if you have any feedback or questions.

Hi /v/books, I'm wondering what your personal opinions are on the reading order for the Dune series. I recently finished Dune and Dune Messiah, but with all the books out now I was curious if there were a better order to read them in besides publishing order.

thanks!

To be frank, I found that the further you got from the original work the further the drop in quality =/ That being said, I enjoyed the first few of the main series, but IMHO after Children of Dune it starts to take a turn for the wacky. As for the extended (read: profit whoring) universe... the prequels are OK at best, so long as you don't really expect award winning quality form them. I would recommend reading those after the main series as they are meant to fill in references from the main story. I have not read the House series (House Atreides, House Harkonnen, etc.) as I was already kinda feeling burned by the extended series, so I can't really make much of a recommendation there.

TL;DR: If you are looking for more awesome like the original stay with the first few books of the main series, if you don't mind mediocre and just want more of the universe, go ahead and check out the spinoffs but I would say read them after.

Anyhoo, does anyone use hybrid hard drives? Mostly SATA with a small SSD for regular programs. Supposed to be quick, but I just wondered how much quicker than a normal drive for gaming use.

I'm pretty sure the consensus is that they aren't really worth it, except maybe if you're limited to a single drive bay. For example, Newegg's cheapest has 8GB of NAND and 1TB of HDD space for $80. On the other hand, you can get a 1TB HDD for $45 and a 60GB SSD for $35. This way, you get more total storage, and more of it is fast flash memory. You can even find 240-256GB SSDs for $80 now if you want to sacrifice a little bit of space for some more super-fast storage.

I have one in my laptop, because it's only the one drive bay and it needed a new hard drive. It's probably not going to improve your gaming experience.

Ultimately, the hybrid drive is a compromise. It seems a little faster than the plain spinning-rust I had been using, but it's not as fast as the SSD in my desktop. It has a good amount of storage space, but it's less than non-hybrid drives. It's a compromise that was worth making when I bought it and SSDs were much more expensive per GB and I needed the space and I wanted more speed. Today, I would buy an SSD for the same job, because prices have come down. And, in my recent gaming build, I didn't have to compromise because I had more than one drive bay.

I'm limited to a single drive bay on my main rig, and I got a 1TB/(8GB) Seagate hybrid drive on sale for cheaper than a regular Seagate 1TB. It boots ridiculously fast (compared to my old 7200rpm 500gb) and I have plenty of storage.

BTW, AFAIK, the partitions are combined. The first 8GB of files written to the drive are put on the flash, the rest on the platter.

Usually when I have used hybrid drives in the past they have been in laptops. This makes more sense because there usually is not room for two drives in a laptop. When building desktops I would always go SSD for OS and a HDD for storage.
